title: Route Elevation Gain Calculator: Total Climb

faq: How accurate is the gain?
It is computed from terrain data sampled at 40 points along the routed path. Longer routes smooth small bumps; the total is a sound planning figure, not a surveyor's audit.
Walking only?
The time estimate is a walking one (Naismith-flavoured), but the gain and loss describe the terrain for any traveller — cyclists and runners use the same numbers.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Mountains are indifferent to traffic.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
The path sampled is the routed one — the climb belongs to the ground you will actually cross.
Can route results change over time?
Terrain data improves in resolution over the years; a re-run can refine a figure slightly. The hill itself is patient.
Gain and loss are both shown — why?
Descents cost knees and time too, and on a point-to-point the loss can exceed the gain. Both totals describe the day.
What is elevation range?
Highest minus lowest point on the route — the vertical span, distinct from the accumulated gain. A high plateau scores range without much gain.
Is descent ever the bigger number?
On point-to-point routes off a plateau, yes — loss can exceed gain, and your knees will file the report either way.
Does gain include the little dips?
Sampling at 40 points captures the shape at that resolution; gravel-path ripples below it are smoothed, honestly and by design.
How does gain relate to calories?
Climbing is work against gravity; more gain, more energy. The cycling calorie model elsewhere prices distance only — add your own hill surcharge.
